Badawi Urges Sustained Oil and Gas Investment to Safeguard International Energy Supply
Egypt’s Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi urged continued investment in oil and natural gas exploration, production and infrastructure to bolster energy security during the 17th ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum (IEF) in Riyadh, according to a statement by the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources (MoPMR).
Badawi stressed that energy security is a shared responsibility and cannot be achieved without sufficient investment in the oil and gas industries, calling for greater spending on exploration, production, infrastructure and technology.
Badawi outlined Egypt’s priorities for securing its energy needs, including increasing domestic oil and natural gas production by improving the investment climate and accelerating exploration, drilling and field development in cooperation with investment partners. He added that Egypt aimed to maximize the economic value of its petroleum resources by increasing refinery utilization and expanding petrochemical production and other value-added products.
The minister said natural gas remained a key component of Egypt’s energy mix, supporting electricity supply as the country integrated more renewable energy capacity, adding that Egypt is working to diversify supply sources, improve energy efficiency, rationalize consumption and expand renewable energy, while exploring emerging options such as hydrogen.
He sheds light on measures taken to improve the investment climate in the oil and natural gas sector, including settling outstanding payments to foreign partners, introducing new investment incentives, improving investment terms and making geological data and exploration opportunities more accessible through digital platforms such as the Egypt Upstream Gateway (EUG).
On the importance of regional cooperation and infrastructure connecting production sources with consumption centers and international market citing Cyprus’s Cronos gas field as an example of regional cooperation, noting that the project would enable Cypriot natural gas to be transported to Egypt for processing and liquefaction before being exported to European markets.
He added that the model could be extended to other Eastern Mediterranean resources, including Cyprus’s Aphrodite field and discoveries in Block 10.
The IEF’s 17th ministerial meeting was held in Riyadh, the Saudi Arabian capital, on October 11 under the theme “Energy Security and Shared Goals in a New Era.” The meeting was inaugurated by Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and IEF Secretary-General Jassim al-Shirawi.

IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures
Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year
John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.
As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.
Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.
Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”
‘Costing billions’: is the pensions triple lock a lifeline or simply unaffordable?
Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt , the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.
Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review.
“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.
Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”
Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.
“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”
Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.
With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.
Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.
The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.
However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.
Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.
The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.
“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.
“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”
She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.
A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.
“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

items.title: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine 'Holiday Hunger Bill'
items.summary: The education minister has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.
items.content:
Image caption, Paul Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect
Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food.
The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn FÃ©in assembly member Danny Baker.
Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department Â£20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.
The Holiday Meals Payment Bill , external would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food.
The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday.
Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation.
He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted.
It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal.
Image caption, The payment would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food
As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education.
It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families Â£27 per child every fortnight.
In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it.
He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect.
A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin".
They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands."

items.content:
At the height of the recent crisis in the Middle East, the collapse of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted 14% of global oil and natural gas supply. Bypass pipelines, additional production and stock drawdowns covered more than half of the shortfall; lower consumption accounted for the rest. But not every country had the same room to maneuver. Those with ample reserves, alternative suppliers and the means to absorb higher costs could ride out the shock, while the rest competed for fewer, costlier cargo.
This disparity is central to “Aftershocks,” a study published on September 17 by the McKinsey Global Institute. It assesses 65 economies by their exposure to supply disruptions and their capacity to respond. The surge in freight rates pointed to the binding constraint: deliverability, not availability. A cargo of crude oil, refined products or LNG needs a suitable vessel, insurance and safe passage, and refining, storage or regasification capacity at its destination.
Greece already controls key links in this supply chain, possessing the world’s largest merchant fleet by carrying capacity, refineries and storage facilities, ports, and shipbuilding and repair yards. The EU’s Operation Aspides, whose area of operations has extended from the Red Sea to the Strait of Hormuz since 2024, is run from Larissa. Brussels’ maritime and ports strategies, adopted in March, treat such capabilities as integral to economic security, resilience and defense. What Greece still lacks is a permanent mechanism for coordination between the state and the shipping industry when supply chains break down.
Norway has relied on such a framework for decades. In 1940, its government assumed control of most of the merchant fleet outside German-controlled areas. The model was revived during the Cold War and took its present form in 2002 as Nortraship, a standing body linking government and shipowners, with an operational role in crises. When the war in Iran choked off energy flows, the security and preparedness department of the Norwegian Shipowners’ Association worked with the authorities and DNK, Norway’s war-risk insurer, to assess threats and keep companies informed. With that support, every Norwegian-linked vessel seeking to leave the Persian Gulf was out by the end of June.
A comparable Greek arrangement would provide real-time situational awareness of which Greek-owned vessels, by location, commitments and insurance cover, are available for charter in a supply emergency. It would speed their mobilization and the flow of security information, and track the status of ports, storage facilities, refineries and shipyards. Mobilization, however, depends on insurance: During the crisis, private underwriters canceled or sharply repriced war-risk cover, prompting Washington to announce a state-backed reinsurance facility. In May, an EU official stated that the bloc was considering state guarantees to help shipping companies with premiums, but no such EU initiative has yet been announced.
With Greek owners accounting for about three-fifths of the EU-controlled fleet, Athens has more at stake than any other member-state, and more standing to make the case for such an instrument in Brussels.

Saudi Arabian Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud has received a phone call from his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, the Saudi state news agency reported.
The two ministers discussed the recent escalations in the region after the Houthis, backed by Iran, attacked Saudi airports.

list 2 of 3 Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?

In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Araghchi emphasised that insisting on a military approach while disregarding political solutions would further complicate the situation. The Iranian minister said the region’s crises have no military solutions. Last week, Araghchi said “there is no military solution” to the US war, adding, “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict.
Araghchi said Iran is ready to provide any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and to help achieve a political solution.
Following the deadly attack on the Riyadh airport that killed 12 people and wounded 300, US President Donald Trump said he would reconsider the US role in Yemen, adding that he is weighing resuming strikes on Iran.
These remarks represent a departure from the president’s comments on Thursday that Washington will not resume strikes on Iran until after the US midterm elections.
Iranian and Saudi diplomatic ties have endured despite longstanding friction, with embassies restored under a 2023 Chinese-brokered agreement remaining operational. Before that breakthrough, a seven-year diplomatic rupture had fuelled regional proxy conflicts.
Riyadh’s relationship with Tehran has deteriorated since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February. Following the attacks, Tehran and its aligned forces have struck  US military assets and energy infrastructure across the Gulf region, including oil fields in Saudi Arabia.
In March 2026, Prince Faisal warned Iran that tolerance of its attacks on Saudi Arabia and those of neighbouring Gulf states is limited, calling on Tehran to “recalculate” its strategy.

items.title: Not Nvidia. Not Broadcom. This Little-Known Chip Supplier Could Be the AI Boom's Best-Kept Secret. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Not Nvidia. Not Broadcom. This Little-Known Chip Supplier Could Be the AI Boom's Best-Kept Secret.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
When investors think about the artificial intelligence boom, two names tend to dominate conversations. They are Nvidia ( NVDA -0.52% ) , which supplies the graphics processing units (GPUs) powering much of the AI industry, and Broadcom ( AVGO +0.39% ) , which helps tech companies develop custom silicon. But there's a lesser-known player that could be the industry's best-kept secret: Cerebras Systems ( CBRS -2.23% ) .
With Cerebras, it all starts with speed. Instead of the usual approach to chip design, Cerebras built its business around a large processor designed specifically for artificial intelligence : its Wafer-Scale Engine.
The chip combines computing cores, memory, and communication capabilities into a single piece of silicon, reducing the need to move data between separate components. Through this approach, Cerebras aims to alleviate bottlenecks that can slow AI workloads.
That matters because training an AI model is only one part of the equation. Once a model is deployed, it's used for AI inference , answering questions, writing code, and even executing tasks for millions of users in real time. In fact, inference is becoming one of the fastest-growing trends in the AI market today.
Cerebras is investing in that shift by working to make AI responses faster.
As AI applications become more interactive, speed could become a huge competitive advantage. It could make conversations with AI chatbots faster and more fluid, while enabling AI agents to complete multi-step tasks more quickly, across domains ranging from software development and business workflows to scientific research.
The company's approach is already attracting attention from major AI players, including OpenAI.
Getting a major AI company to adopt its technology is a huge vote of confidence for any chipmaker. That's why Cerebras' relationship with OpenAI stands out.
The companies recently announced a multi-year agreement to deploy 750 megawatts of Cerebras compute capacity for OpenAI customers, with deployment planned in stages through 2028. The goal is to make AI responses faster, particularly for workloads that generate long answers, assist with coding, and power AI agents.
The partnership took an even bigger turn in August, when Cerebras announced that it's powering the Ultrafast mode for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. The company says the service can deliver up to 750 output tokens per second and run up to 14 times faster than with standard processing. This demonstrates how Cerebras' specialized hardware can greatly improve the user experience with advanced AI models.
For investors, the important point is that Cerebras' technology is already powering real commercial AI services, backed by one of the leading AI model providers. But proving its technology works is only part of the equation.
The company is also racing to build out its next-generation hardware.
Cerebras recently announced its CS-4 system, which it says can deliver up to twice the speed of its predecessor, along with improved efficiency and faster token generation. CS-4 is part of a broader platform that Cerebras says will allow it to upgrade computing, cooling, and power delivery more independently. That matters because performance doesn't depend on chips alone.
Data centers must also deliver enough power, move data efficiently, and cool dense hardware. As a result, by adopting this design, the company is trying to improve the economics of running AI at scale. That makes Cerebras' technology better suited for large deployments, especially as AI data centers become bigger and more complex.
For investors looking beyond the biggest chipmakers, this continued product development is another reason to watch the company.

Nvidia and Broadcom may be providing much of the infrastructure behind AI, but the AI boom is also creating opportunities for lesser-known chipmakers. That could mean room for more than one winning chip design.
Looking ahead, Cerebras' focus on speed and inference could give it a major role in the next phase of the AI boom, especially as it launches broader platforms that can scale with AI data centers.
If demand for faster AI keeps growing, Cerebras could turn out to be one of the market's strongest under-the-radar chip suppliers.
